articles.title: 2 more B.C. Conservative MLAs quit caucus to sit as Independents
articles.summary: Donegal Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen, and Scott McInnis, MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke, have have quit the B.C. Conservative caucus.

image.caption: Donegal Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen, says she is stepping away from the B.C. Conservative caucus sit as an Independent. (Legislative Assembly of B.C.)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Donegal Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen, and Scott McInnis, MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke, have have quit the B.C. Conservative caucus.
Donegal Wilson, Scott McInnis says she has lost confidence in new party leader

The Conservative Party of B.C. has lost two more MLAs as Donegal Wilson and Scott McInnis became the eighth and ninth members to quit caucus in recent weeks, both citing concerns about party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay's leadership.
"I never imagined things could go this wrong, this quickly," Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen, said in a statement.

Wilson, who was elected in 2024, said she remains a conservative in principle but added that communication within the party had broken down and she has worries about the direction under Findlay, particularly around staffing decisions.
McInnis, MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke, said in a separate statement that he no longer supports "the direction, judgment and decisions of Kerry-Lynne Findlay's leadership."

"The party has increasingly become an exclusive private club more concerned with ideological bona fides than building the broad coalition required to serve British Columbians and form government," he said.

Wilson and McInnis follow seven other MLAs to step away from the Conservatives, the latest being Á'a:líya Warbus, MLA for Chilliwack-Cultus Lake, who on Monday also said she had lost confidence in Findlay.

items: More stories from the B.C. Interior
Can Kerry-Lynne Findlay keep B.C. Conservatives together amid caucus turmoil?

blocks.text: The B.C. Conservative caucus said in a statement that it remains focused on its work as the Official Opposition to "[hold] the NDP government accountable and restoring prosperity for the people of this province."
Findlay will run in a byelection triggered by Conservative MLA for Abbotsford-Mission Reann Gasper's decision to step down from her role to allow the Conservative leader to seek a seat.
Findlay said the criticisms by departing members of her caucus are baseless.
"What we are seeing is a co-ordinated political attack designed to sidetrack our campaign at the very moment we are taking our message directly to the people of Abbotsford-Mission," she said.

Findlay said she has spent her career in positions of significant public trust, including as a lawyer, a former Canadian Human Rights Tribunal judge, a King's Counsel, a member of the King's Privy Council for Canada and as a federal cabinet minister.
The B.C. Conservatives' chief of staff Chris Delaney also resigned Wednesday.
Findlay named Gasper as her new chief of staff. Gasper had served as deputy chief of staff after stepping down as MLA.

items: B.C. Conservative Party campaign manager, executive director steps down
B.C. Conservative president out as party transitions under new leadership

blocks.text: Findlay was elected as party leader in May. Since then, the party has lost key staffers and faced allegations that she attempted to induce MLAs to step down to open a seat for her in the B.C. Legislature, a claim which she has denied as a political smear.
Two ex-Conservatives, Peter Milobar and Ian Paton, say they intend to form a new party.
With files from Lauren Vanderdeen, Katie DeRosa and Simon Little

articles.title: Israel ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’
articles.summary:
Defence minister says he believes US backing could tip regional balance in favour of forced resettlement

Israel’s defence minister has said his country is seeking Donald Trump’s support to…

blocks.text: Israel’s defence minister has said his country is seeking Donald Trump’s support to approve plans to expel Palestinians from the Gaza Strip in what has widely been condemned as a potential war crime.

Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration” during a conference hosted by the Israeli news site Ynet and the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth. He said the Israeli government was “organised and prepared to get them out by sea, by air, by every way possible”.

Trump discussed a US takeover of the Gaza Strip in early 2025 that would have involved removing Palestinians from the territory, but has since pulled back from the idea. A 20-point peace plan the White House drew up last year did not call for Palestinians’ deportation, an act that would be widely seen as ethnic cleansing.

blocks.caption: Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said removal of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip was ‘being discussed all the time’. Photograph: Israeli Defence Ministry/Reuters

blocks.text: Katz, however, said on Wednesday that he believed US support could tip regional opinion in favour of the forced resettlement of Palestinians from Gaza. He said Trump’s approval was crucial to convince neighbouring countries to accept Palestinian refugees.
“Every country that is willing to take them in wants American backing,” he said. “Trump has not cancelled this at the moment. He has frozen it.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request from the Guardian for comment on whether Trump was continuing to hold discussions on Israel’s proposals to forcibly depopulate the Gaza Strip.

Katz pointed in particular to Egypt, which he said had lobbied Washington to oppose the forced removal of the Palestinian population. “It has not been cancelled,” he said. “It is being discussed all the time, including now, and I think there is no other solution in the end that is in everyone’s interest.”

The remarks come during a competitive election season in Israel in which the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his rightwing allies have appealed to voters by calling for more aggressive measures against Palestinians.

Some have been openly inflammatory and cruel. The far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, posted footage on X from a women’s prison where he said he was responsible for the dire conditions in the facility.

When one prisoner told him they were not receiving medical care, showering or receiving clean clothing, Ben-Gvir said: “The good conditions in the prisons are over. This is the current situation, and I am directly responsible for everything. I am pleased with these conditions.”

Netanyahu visited an Israeli military post close to the yellow line in the Gaza Strip on Wednesday. Israel has said it would not pull back from that line until Hamas disarmed, despite calls for a phased withdrawal to facilitate a recent ceasefire with the group.

“We control the territory and are staying on this line,” Netanyahu said. “We are doing everything to achieve our goal – disarming Hamas and demilitarising Gaza. Gaza will no longer pose a threat to Israel.”

articles.title: Arrest warrants issued in Mexico for duo accused in alleged condo scam
articles.summary: A Mexican court has issued arrest warrants against the man and woman accused of defrauding a Canadian couple of their retirement savings through an alleged condo-flip scheme, CBC News has learned.

image.caption: Harry Robinson, left, and Jacqueline Herrera Herrera, right, are accused of defrauding an Ontario couple out of $280,000 with a condo-flipping scheme in Mexico. (Harry Robinson/Facebook; Jacqueline Herrera Herrera/Facebook)

blocks.text: World·New
A Mexican court has issued arrest warrants against the man and woman accused of defrauding a Canadian couple of their retirement savings through an alleged condo-flip scheme, CBC News has learned.
Ontario couple put $280K into plan to flip condos in Playa del Carmen
The warrants for Harry Robinson, a British national, and Jacqueline Herrera Herrera, a Mexican national, were issued in late July by a Quintana Roo state court judge.
Both are now before a Mexican federal court seeking to toss those warrants, according to copies of court records.
The criminal case against them, which is being heard at the state level, won’t be impacted by the federal court process around the arrest warrants, however.
Robinson and Herrera are accused by the state prosecutor's office of committing fraud through deception.

The Canadian couple — Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown, of Curve Lake, Ont. — sent $280,000 to a company co-owned by a Robinson and Herrera who promised big returns on a condo flip in Playa del Carmen that never materialized.
"It is not something that leaves your mind because you’re always worried about what’s going to happen, what’s next," said Thompson this week.
Quintana Roo is a popular vacation and investment destination for Canadians, and also home to Cancun and Tulum.
Thompson and Brown filed a criminal complaint against Robinson and Herrera earlier this year.
The case stems from late 2024 when Thompson, searching for possible real estate investments in Mexico, came across the web page for XMEX Investments which was run by Robinson.
She eventually met Robinson and Herrera in Playa del Carmen. Herrera pitched her on buying a one-bedroom condo and Thompson sent $170,000 in two installments, but never received the keys.
Robinson then convinced Thompson to move her money, with an additional $110,000 from Brown, into a deal to flip seven condos, saying via WhatApp it was looking "to be 100 per cent profit."
Thompson and Brown’s money then vanished.
A federal court judge granted a stay on Aug. 27 against the warrant seeking Herrera’s arrest, but the process to have it tossed continues, according to court records.
A hearing on Robinson’s application is scheduled for Sept. 8 in Cancun, according to court records.
Herrera has claimed in WhatsApp messages that Robinson took some of the money. Robinson filed a criminal complaint against Herrera in late 2025 alleging she stole all the money.

items: Mexican authorities probe alleged scam that wiped out Canadian couple’s retirement savings
U.S. may seek win with Mexico in wake of collapsed trade talks with Canada, says ex-negotiator

blocks.text: Neither Robinson, Herrera’s lawyer in Cancun nor the state deputy-prosecutor who is leading the case responded to a request for comment.

Herrera, through another lawyer, offered a cash settlement in early August to Thompson for about $2.3 million pesos, roughly $188,000, according to WhatsApp text and voice messages obtained by CBC News.
She then offered Thompson a commercial property in Cancun which she claimed was worth about $4 million pesos, or roughly $328,000.
Thompson rejected the offers.
"We're not going to get into any deals like that with her, ever again," said Thompson.
She says it’s been frustrating trying to understand the complex workings of the Mexican judicial system and the various moving parts associated with the case.
"I'm a little more hopeful, although today, my anxiety's through the roof," said Thompson. "It's hard not being there and not really knowing firsthand what’s going on."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jorge Barrera is a Caracas-born journalist currently based in Mexico City for CBC News. He previously worked with CBC's Investigative Unit and CBC's Indigenous Unit. Follow him on X @JorgeBarrera or email him jorge.barrera@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Maltese tycoon found not guilty of involvement in Daphne Caruana Galizia murder
articles.summary:
Yorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrage

One of Malta’s richest men has been found not guilty of involvement in the murder…

blocks.text: One of Malta’s richest men has been found not guilty of involvement in the murder of the anti-corruption journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

The verdict, which is expected to be appealed against by the prosecution, will come as a blow not only to the victim’s family, but to the politicians and campaigners who regard the case as a landmark action in the fight to protect press freedom in Europe.

Nearly nine years after Caruana Galizia’s death, aged 53, in a car bombing in October 2017, a jury of six women and three men found Yorgen Fenech, 44, not guilty of both counts with which he had been charged: complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, and association with the intention of committing a crime.

The verdict was decisive. As family members and the media watched, the forewoman announced the verdict to gasps and cheers, saying the jurors had voted to dismiss both counts by an eight to one majority.

Fenech, an influential businessman and property developer whose family owns two Hilton hotels and has a share in a power station in Malta, had been accused by prosecutors of paying €150,000 via a middle man, Melvin Theuma, to have the journalist killed. Prosecutors had asked for him to be sentenced to life in prison.

blocks.caption: A person holds up an image of Caruana Galizia at a protest in Valletta in 2019. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters

blocks.text: The murder of Caruana Galizia, who targeted Fenech and leading political figures in her reporting, triggered the most consequential political scandal in Malta’s postwar history, becoming a rallying point for anti-corruption and press freedom activism.
The fallout resulted in Joseph Muscat, the then prime minister of the EU’s smallest member state, being forced out of office along with two of his ministers and his chief of staff.

The two-month trial laid bare the extent of Fenech’s network of political contacts, and raised questions about attempts to sabotage and interfere with the police investigation. Key witnesses, and the defendant himself, claimed the prime minister’s chief of staff had repeatedly leaked sensitive information to Fenech.

Summing up the case against him, the prosecutor Anthony Vella said Fenech believed he could “buy justice”, telling the jury: “You are being asked to decide whether a man who had extensive contacts in politics and among the heads of public entities had enough power to pay for Daphne to be killed.”

The defence argued that the chain of command went higher, with suggestions from Fenech and his lawyers that the person who had ordered the killing was Muscat’s former chief of staff Keith Schembri. They said police had not done enough to investigate allegations about his involvement.
after newsletter promotion
“All roads lead to Keith, and all bridges to Keith were burned,” the defence lawyer Charles Mercieca said in his summing up.

In his testimony, Fenech told the jury: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder”. He said he had merely acted as a messenger between Schembri and Theuma, and that the taxi-driver had blackmailed him.
Schembri, who gave evidence at the trial, denied all wrongdoing, saying he had no involvement in leaks and no knowledge of the murder.

articles.title: Berlin's punitive measures unlikely to deter Putin: experts
articles.summary: Germany has announced punitive measures after publicly blaming Russia for an attempted airport drone attack. But a former diplomat, political and security analysts warn it will likely do little to…

image.caption: Speaking on Tuesday, President Putin called Germany's response 'another mistake, a serious one' with the Kremlin vowing to respond 'in kind' Image: Florian Gaertner/photothek/picture alliance

blocks.text: The practical impact of Germany's latest measures against Russia may be limited, according to Russian political scientist Dmitry Oreshkin, who described the response as largely symbolic.

However, Berlin's decision to publicly attribute the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4 to Moscow reflects a growing willingness to respond to Russian President Vladimir Putin and what Berlin sees as hostile actions on its territory.

"It's only a source of joy for Putin. After all, he is restoring this Iron Curtain between Russia and all the other countries. And now he's getting help from the other side as well," Oreshkin told DW. "Putin is someone who cannot be stopped by anything other than escalation and tough restrictions."
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig

Berlin's decision to close the Russian consulate in the western city of Bonn, terminate the contract for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and tighten entry controls for Russian citizens does not go far enough, according to Boris Bondarev, a former diplomat who worked for the Russian permanent mission to the UN Office at Geneva.

Bondarev, who resigned his post in 2022 over Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, said reducing staff and restricting diplomatic activities may complicate Russian operations in Germany, but they will not fundamentally alter Moscow's strategic calculus.

"I'm not sure this will be perceived in Russia as something that will make them think twice," he said. "Unless there are other, more coordinated steps at the EU level, they won't stop provocations. At most, they may force them to coordinate a little differently and look for more professional operatives."
Both experts agreed, however, that Germany's measures could have an effect even if they fail to deter Moscow — by setting off another cycle of reciprocal restrictions.
How will Russia respond?
Speaking on Tuesday, President Putin called Germany's response "another mistake, a serious one," with the Kremlin telling the German Press Agency that Russia would respond "in kind."

German security policy expert Wolfgang Richter said the risk of escalation has increased compared with the early years of the Russia-Ukraine war, but said the next phase of confrontation between Berlin and Moscow is likely to remain in the areas of diplomacy and culture.

"They will, for example, close the Goethe-Institut," said Richter, a colonel with Germany's military until his retirement in 2010. "I would not quite exclude that they could also escalate a little bit and do more — for example, limit the number of diplomats in the German embassy in Moscow."
Former diplomat Bondarev, however, said the Kremlin's reaction could be difficult to predict.

"Moscow officials can surprise you. They could say: 'We have all these people under surveillance anyway, so why expel them? Let them work, and we'll continue monitoring them.' It could go either way. But most likely, there will be some high-profile retaliatory steps," he said.
Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid

The dispute over organizations such as the Goethe-Institut and the Russian House in Berlin reflects a deeper divide in how Moscow and Western governments view their role. The Goethe-Institut, founded in 1951 to promote German language and culture abroad, is seen by Moscow through the lens of its broader suspicion of Western institutions, said Oreshkin. And, he added, the Kremlin tends to assume that such organizations serve intelligence purposes because it projects its own security-service worldview onto Western structures.

"The Russian system of thinking among the security services assumes that all Western institutions are organized in exactly the same way. This symmetrical picture of the world is deeply mistaken," he said.
Oreshkin said it's unlikely the Kremlin will escalate much further than the level of diplomacy and culture.

"Launching a missile strike — that's something Putin doesn't have the guts to do. And all these acts of sabotage and subversion — supporting alternative political movements, like Alternative for Germany — they're already doing that anyway," he said. "So I don't think Putin can escalate much beyond that. He can, in fact, escalate the rhetoric, and that's what he's doing."
Real pressure point: Russia's shadow fleet

Announcing the measures on Monday, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks." That included tougher action against Russia's "shadow fleet," though he didn't provide further details.
Russian officials have repeatedly warned that attempts to detain or seize vessels linked to Russia's network of ships ​accused of circumventing fuel sanctions would be regarded as hostile acts.
NATO listens underwater to guard against Russian sabotage

Oreshkin said if Europe really wants to put pressure on the Kremlin, targeting the financial flows behind the shadow fleet would be more effective. But he pointed to a major obstacle: European governments are constrained by their own legal frameworks, which include maritime law that ensure freedom of navigation.

Security expert Richter, however, sees a broader security risk. Pressure on the shadow fleet could increase the likelihood of incidents at sea, he told DW. "And that would, of course, mean another escalation."

For Richter, the answer lies in making sure both sides understand the risks involved. "The situation has become more tense and it's high time to speak," he said. Without communication between the parties, he warned, any actions could be misinterpreted and might trigger further escalation.

articles.title: Unity at last: Is Libya's damaging power struggle at an end?
articles.summary: For over a decade, Libya has been split between two opposing governments. Elections, meant to end the rivalry and unite the country, are now scheduled within two years.

image.caption: On the road to democracy? Local elections were held in Libya in August 2025Image: Mahmud Turkia/AFP

blocks.text: There have been other attempts made in the past but this time, those involved hope it will finally work out: Thanks to mediation by the United Nations, the two opposing governments in the west and east of Libya have agreed that they will hold parliamentary and presidential elections within the next two years.
"The agreement marks an important step in advancing Libya towards national elections and ending the transitional period," the UN's Support Mission in Libya, or UNSMIL, said in a statement.

Among other things, the country's electoral commission will be restructured and, according to the UN, various points about the legal framework for the elections that had previously led to disagreements have now been resolved.
But whether all this will actually result in free and fair elections in Libya remains to be seen.
Divided for over a decade
After former Libyan dictator Moammar Gadhafi was overthrown in 2011, Libya ended up divided in two.

Since 2014, the country has been split between opposing governments located in the east and west of the country. A UN-backed administration known as the Government of National Unity is based in Tripoli in the west, and its rival, known as the House of Representatives, is based in the east, in Tobruk.
Former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar, is based in the east while Prime Minister Abdul-Hamid Dbeibah is in charge in the west.

Each is supported by a number of local militias and foreign powers, and each has tried to wrest control from the other. Up until now, attempts to hold an election that would unite the country have failed.
For Andreas Dittmann, a geographic conflict expert and professor at the University of Giessen in Hesse, central Germany, the apparent unity is a positive.
"Things could not continue the way they were," he told DW.

After years of civil war and political division, the desire of many Libyans to end the fighting permanently has only grown. Dittmann believes the attitudes of political actors have also changed in this regard.

Previously foreign actors had supported just one Libyan government, but now that has also changed and the prevailing argument seems to be that Libya can only develop further if both sides are incorporated into one administration.

This is why the UN is trying to go beyond simply arranging a date for elections. It also wants to strengthen the electoral commission and work on electoral laws. The new and united government will be responsible for establishing the conditions for a secure and trusted electoral process.
The UN has also set up what it calls "Structured Dialogues," during which consensus was sought on questions of leadership, security, the economy and reconciliation.
Past agreements didn't work out

Michael Bauer, who heads the Tunisia office of Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, believes the agreement is an important, if limited, step. Its success will depend on how binding any decisions are, he argued.
After all, Bauer said, there have been plenty of political agreements in Libya in the recent past but none were really ever implemented.

Parallel to the UN process, the US is also trying to work on bringing the disparate leadership together. Massad Boulos, the Trump administration's senior adviser on Arab and Middle Eastern affairs, has been trying to bring the Dbeibah and Haftar families together.

blocks.caption: Libya is potentially a rich country due to its mineral resources and large oil reservesImage: Hussein Malla/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In June, Haftar's son Saddam was in Washington where he met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Bauer said the American way of dealing with Libya differentiates from the UN plan. "While the UN mission has basically been very inclusive, in my opinion, the American mission is trying to bring about a kind of deal between the country's elites," he told DW.
He questions how such a deal would fit into free and fair elections in Libya.
"Elections can only be meaningful if the outcome has not already been decided beforehand," Bauer said. The same is true for any pre-election allocation of political positions.
Elites strike a deal?

UK-based think tank Chatham House has already warned that a deal like this, around ministries and resources, will only institutionalize the existing rivalry between Libya's ruling elites. With such an arrangement the rival actors would just divide the state's resources between themselves, and corruption and patronage systems would continue.
The country's division into east and west will be hard to overcome. A new united government would have to deal with preexisting power structures, rather than starting anew.

Dittmann said there is a further problem. Much of the Libyan population lives in the western areas, especially in the Tripoli region. This would see the eastern half of the country lose power if elections are held.

blocks.caption: Locals hope for economic growth and stabilityImage: Islam Alatrash/DW

blocks.text: "If there are elections, and if those elections proceed mostly according to democratic principles, then the east can really only lose," he explained.
Additionally, there are also external actors to consider. Russia has extended its positioning in the east while Turkey supports the government in the west.
Alongside all of that is also the question of what the Libyan people want and what they expect from a united government. Bauer doubts elections alone can resolve Libya's problems.
"The people have a particular interest in seeing the country's dysfunction end," he said.

Libya is rich in raw materials and energy reserves, but also plagued by problems like power outages and inadequate public services. If the state was functioning properly, it would likely curtail the power of those currently benefiting most from the country's resources and, as Bauer argued, "why would they voluntarily give up these opportunities?"

That will be the most difficult question for the next two years. The new agreement between Libya's political rivals must do more than simply establish a path toward elections. It must also create a framework in which those rivals accept the results of an election and in which public institutions function properly.
This story was originally written in German.

articles.title: Iranian attack on Saudi tanker killed two Filipino sailors, Saudi Arabia says
articles.summary: The kingdom condemns the targeting of Sidr, which was reportedly hit by unknown projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday.

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia has condemned what it said was an Iranian attack on a Saudi-owned supertanker on Monday night that killed two Filipino sailors.
The Saudi national shipping company, Bahri, confirmed on Wednesday that its vessel Sidr was "involved in a security incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz".

Sidr was hit by projectiles north of Oman's Musandam Peninsula, according to maritime security firms. A South Korean-owned supertanker, Senegal Prosperity, was reportedly struck east of Musandam around the same time.
Iran has not responded to the Saudi allegation. But it said earlier that two tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while using an unauthorised route through the strait.

The news of the sailors' deaths came after the US military carried out a wave of air strikes on Iran and Iranian forces targeted US bases in neighbouring Arab states with missiles and drones in their biggest exchange of fire since July.

On Wednesday Iran's health minister said 18 people were killed and 108 injured in the US attacks. Iran has accused the US of a "war crime" over a strike that killed four people including two children at a wedding party in the southern city of Sirik. The US military said it was looking into the reports.
Shipping company Bahri's statement said the unspecified "security incident" affecting Sidr happened in the Strait of Hormuz at around 23:40 local time (19:40 GMT) on Monday.

"It is with profound sadness that Bahri confirms the loss of two of its Filipino seafarers as a result of the incident," it added. "The company extends its deepest condolences and heartfelt sympathies to their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time."
Later, the Saudi foreign ministry expressed the kingdom's condemnation of "Iran's targeting of the Saudi tanker (Sidr) while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz".

It also condemned the recent Iranian attacks on Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait, and stressed the "need to halt escalation and respect the security and safety of international navigation", as well as the security of global energy supplies, national sovereignty, and international law.

The statements were issued a day after maritime risk management and intelligence firms Marisks and Kpler reported that two tankers each loaded with two million barrels of Saudi crude oil were struck by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other as they transited outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday.

Sidr was struck by "unknown projectiles" at 19:52 GMT about 16 nautical miles (30km) north-east of Khasab, Oman, while Senegal Prosperity was struck by "three unknown projectiles" about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, according to Marisks.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency also reported two incidents in the same locations.

On Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps said in a statement that two oil tankers sought "at the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route" in the Strait of Hormuz before "striking mines and exploding". The vessels were "currently on fire", it added.

The US military has not commented, but it said the latest strikes on Iran followed "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members".

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran in February due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
Despite the Iranian attacks, US President Donald Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said 17 million barrels of oil flowed through the Strait of Hormuz by ship on Monday - a record daily total since the start of the war.

articles.title: 'I don't feel like a hero,' says Winnipeg woman who saved father, drowning toddler from Red River
articles.summary: A Winnipeg woman says she's still recovering, but glad everyone is safe, days after rescuing both a child who fell into the Red River and the girl's father, who attempted to save the child.

image.caption: Jayclyn Morrissette says she was on a walk with her neighbour at St. John's Park in Winnipeg last week when noticed a toddler 'flailing' in the Red River. (Submitted by Jayclyn Morrissette)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Updated
A Winnipeg woman says she's still recovering, but glad everyone is safe, days after rescuing both a child who fell into the Red River and the girl's father, who attempted to save the child.
'Selfless' woman jumped into action to save girl who fell into river near St. John's Park, police say
Jayclyn Morrissette, 32, was on a walk with her neighbour at St. John's Park, in Winnipeg's North End, on the evening of Aug. 24.
They stopped at a bench overlooking the Red River, where she "noticed a little girl flailing in the water," Morrissette told CBC on Wednesday.
She went down to the water as her neighbour went to the child's parents, who were frantically searching for the toddler, she said.
"I got down to the edge when the father had jumped in, and it took about 10 seconds before I realized he was not coming back up. So I … emptied my pockets and jumped in."
Trying to rescue the father was difficult, Morrissette said, so her neighbour grabbed her as she held onto him, and they were able to get the man out of the water.
Morrissette then swam back out to get the drowning toddler.
In a Wednesday morning news release detailing the incident, Winnipeg police said the rescuer swam backward toward the riverbank with the unconscious child on her chest.
"When I pulled her out, she was lifeless," Morrissette said. "As I was swimming back, I was also pumping her stomach."

items: Person in stable condition after being rescued from Red River in Winnipeg Thursday

blocks.text: Morrisette says she and her neighbour performed CPR — which she learned over a decade ago —on the child before first responders arrived.
The girl was taken to hospital in critical condition, where she was later stabilized, police said. She is now expected to make a full recovery.
But Morrissette said she suffered nightmares in the days following the incident.
"Her eyes were open and her tongue was purple, so that's all I could see every time I closed my eyes," Morrissette said. "I didn't sleep for a couple of days."

She also says once the adrenaline wore off, she realized she had suffered injuries to her neck and shoulder. She's been taking painkillers and is waiting to get testing, if her injuries do not get better.

Police did not release the child's age nor the names of the people involved, but said in their news release the woman who saved the girl and her father showed "remarkable courage and selflessness" in saving people who were strangers to her, with little regard for her own safety.
"I'm just a mom," Morrissette said. "I don't feel like a hero."
Someone else would have done the same thing in that situation, she said.
"I'm glad I was there. They're lucky I was there. I wish it just never happened," she said.
"Be safe. Watch your kids at all times. It only takes a second."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ozten Shebahkeget is a member of Northwest Angle 33 First Nation who was born and raised in Winnipeg. She started writing for CBC Manitoba during the first Pathways program in 2022. She holds a master's degree in writing from the University of Saskatchewan.

articles.title: Germany: How to woo voters with an immigrant background
articles.summary: The number of voters in Germany with an immigrant background is rising. Yet the established parties barely manage to reach them. Why not?

image.caption: Do centrist parties in Germany not have the right messages for immigrant voters?Image: Emmanuele Contini/IMAGO

blocks.text: German voters of immigrant background are distancing themselves from the established parties even more than others, according to a study by the Berlin-based German Center for Integration and Migration Research (DeZIM).

In 2023, 12% of eligible voters in Germany were of immigration background — meaning they or at least one of their parents were born without German citizenship. That amounts to more than seven million people in a population of close to 84 million. But they are drifting away from the traditional centrist parties.

Nevertheless, according to the study, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) continues to have the greatest voter potential among immigrants and their descendants: Two out of three voters with an immigrant background said they considered the SPD a viable option.
The center-right bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) is close behind in second place. Only one in five respondents categorically rejected these parties.

"Older respondents with an immigrant background lean toward the SPD," said Friederike Römer, co-author of the study, at an online press conference this week. "This bond has been relatively strong in the past, but that seems to be breaking down now among younger generations."
Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough?
AfD targets migrants

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) has the least potential voters of immigrant background. Nearly two-thirds of those surveyed said voting for the far-right was out of the question. People with roots in Turkey, the Middle East, and North Africa, in particular, reject the party, though the AfD does enjoy significant support among Germany's Russian community.

Nevertheless, the AfD is working to win over the immigrant voter base. "For a long time, it was the first party to communicate in immigrants' native languages using images that actually worked," said Martin Gerlach, federal executive director of the Turkish Community in Germany (TGD), recalling the AfD campaign in Berlin during the 2021 federal election. "It read: 'Atatürk would vote for the AfD.' Other parties simply don't bother to think about these target groups. That's crazy, because if you win over big segments of voters with a migration background, you win elections."
Safety a priority for immigrants

The TGD was active in 60 German cities ahead of the last federal election in February 2025, encouraging voters of Turkish background to cast their ballots. But Gerlach has noticed that immigrants are not inherently pro-immigration; on the contrary, there is widespread skepticism toward new immigrants or refugees, an issue that the AfD has seized on. This, he argues, is just one of many reasons why other parties are losing support among those voters.

"The political parties don't address safety at all, and that's a huge issue," he said. "Yet people in our community feel extremely threatened in many parts of Germany — they don't even dare go to the Baltic Sea coast," he added, referring to a series of xenophobic attacks in that region.

Gerlach believes that Islamophobia has a significant effect on voters from the Turkish community, but the centrist parties don't pay enough attention to it. "Anti-discrimination policy is seen in Germany as something progressive and left-wing, yet for the Turkish-origin community, it is about being protected by the constitution in the truest sense of the word," he said. "I believe this is a narrative that could win over a great many people."
Poorly treated? Racism in German medicine
Are the political parties missing a trick on social change?

Political scientist Özgür Özvatan pointed out that by 2030, more than half of Germany's population will have an immigrant background. He has also been critical of the established parties, most recently in his 2025 book "Every Vote Counts — Underestimated by Democrats, Courted by Populists: Migrant Germans as a Political Force."

"They are not reaching out to voters with an immigrant background the way they should — neither to recruit them for their own party, nor as volunteers, nor simply as voters," he said. "Sadly, we're missing the boat with this social change."

Özvatan argues that there is enormous potential to mobilize voters who have moved to Germany from authoritarian countries — people, for example, who have direct experience of trying to defend democracy. "We can tap into that if we enable them to obtain citizenship with voting rights as quickly as possible," he said.

The AfD, meanwhile, relies on a strategy of addressing the Turkish diaspora while establishing connections to the right-wing authoritarian President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. Furthermore, he said, the AfD has become very skilled at pitting people with immigrant backgrounds against one another.

"A great deal of effort is being put into telling older immigrants: 'You are different from the newcomers, this whole debate about migration and deportation won't affect you.' And this tactic works well with those who do not reject the AfD," said Özvatan.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Marcos cites Presidential Airlift Wing
articles.summary: President Marcos has commended the men and women of the 250th Presidential Airlift Wing (PAW) for helping the government swiftly reach and deliver aid to the distressed during times of calamities.

blocks.text: September 3, 2026 | 12:00am

President Marcos joins the Philippine Air Force in celebrating the 58th found- ing anniversary of the 250th Presidential Airlift Wing at Villamor Air Base in Pasay yesterday. The 250th PAW serves as the Air Force’s premier air mobility unit, providing transportation for the President and his family, visiting heads of state and other high-ranking dignitaries.
Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos has commended the men and women of the 250th Presidential Airlift Wing (PAW) for helping the government swiftly reach and deliver aid to the distressed during times of calamities.

Speaking at the 58th anniversary of the PAW yesterday, the President described the unit as the “multiplier” whose continuous training and modernization allowed it to respond safely and effectively to increasingly complex missions, including support for official engagements, emergency response or humanitarian operations.

“In these missions, you do more than just provide transportation. You help the government reach our people when they need us most,” Marcos said at the Philippine Air Force headquarters at the Villamor Air Base in Pasay City, citing his day-long inspection of flooded areas in Central Luzon yesterday.
From the 701st through 707th Special Mission Wing, the 250th PAW now “has been very much state-of-the-art,” the President said.
He presented awards and citations to officers and personnel for their exemplary service.

The 250th PAW is the Air Force’s premier air mobility unit, providing safe, secure, efficient and dignified air transportation for the President, First Family, visiting heads of state and other ranking dignitaries.

articles.title: DepEd to schools: Use AI tool for disaster preparedness
articles.summary: Education Secretary Sonny Angara has ordered public school administrators, teachers and disaster response coordinators nationwide to integrate LIGTAS+ into their disaster preparedness routines as…

blocks.text: September 3, 2026 | 12:00am
Lahar inundates Sta. Fe National High School in San Marcelino, Zambales yesterday.
Noel Pabalete

MANILA, Philippines — Education Secretary Sonny Angara has ordered public school administrators, teachers and disaster response coordinators nationwide to integrate LIGTAS+ into their disaster preparedness routines as hundreds of schools remain affected by flooding and other disasters.

According to Angara, LIGTAS+ or the Learning Institution Geohazard Tracking and Assessment for Safety would allow school leaders to identify risks earlier and make timely decisions before hazards disrupt classes and other school operations.

“We can’t just wait for a storm or earthquake to strike before we act. With LIGTAS+, we can anticipate risks early so our school leaders can make timely, informed decisions before hazards turn into emergencies. What we need is clear and reliable information for earlier preparation,” he said.

Developed by DepEd’s Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Service and the Education Center for AI Research, LIGTAS+ combines artificial intelligence, weather forecasts, satellite radar imagery and data from government and international scientific agencies to provide school-level hazard alerts.

In a separate event, Angara accompanied President Marcos in inspecting flood-affected schools in Tarlac, Zambales and Pampanga, where the combined impact of the southwest monsoon and recent tropical cyclones damaged at least 622 schools and 4,025 classrooms.
Of the damaged classrooms, 946 were destroyed, 806 sustained major damage and 2,274 suffered minor damage.
The DepEd estimated that P2.9 billion would be needed for response and recovery efforts in Central Luzon.

articles.title: Macron visits Bayeux Tapestry with King Charles, PM Andy Burnham
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron is on a shorter-term visit to the UK than the renowned on-loan 11th century tapestry. He viewed the ancient artwork with King Charles and relatively new Prime…

image.caption: The King was due to give a speech before the group went to the unveiling of the exhibit alongside other dignitaries and some schoolchildrenImage: Adrian Dennis/REUTERS

blocks.text: French President Emmanuel Macron began a two-day trip to the UK by visiting another famous new arrival from France, the Bayeux Tapestry, with King Charles III and Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Macron and his wife Brigitte, and Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel joined King Charles and Queen Camilla to walk the length of the 70-meter tapestry in the British Museum.

blocks.caption: The Bayeux Tapestry depicts the events of 1066, a defining date in the passage of British history and in the creation of the modern French-infused English languageImage: Pascal Deloche/Godong/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why is the Bayeux Tapestry in London?

The tapestry, which depicts the momentous events of 1066 culminating in William the Conqueror of Normandy claiming the English throne, is on temporary loan from its usual home in France. It's the first time it's touched British soil since its creation in the 11th century.
The embroidery is on loan for a 10-month exhibiton opening to the public next week, on September 10. The exchange was first announced during Macron's state visit last year.

Though it's thought to have been made in the British Isles, it had been on French soil ever since the 11th century. It's usually on show in Bayeux in Normandy in northern France, hence the name. The effectively priceless artefact was transited across the Channel in secret in July.
Prime Minister Burnham, who took office six weeks ago, called the tapestry's return "a landmark moment" in the history of the two countries.

He also hailed ties with Macron's French government more generally in the House of Commons on Wednesday, alluding to reduced illegal migration crossings of the English Channel — a bid to counter one of Reform UK's favorite summer talking points.
"The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation — the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low," Burnham said.
It's Macron's first UK visit since Burnham took office and their first in-person meeting as leaders.

blocks.caption: Moving the artefact from its usual home in Bayeux to Britain was a painstaking process months in the makingImage: Lou Benoist/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is the Bayeux Tapestry?
The Bayeux Tapestry is a 70-meter long artwork, which is thought to be incomplete, depicting the Norman conquest of England in 1066.

Norman forces led by William the Conqueror were able to defeat and dethrone King Harold Godwinson in a campaign culminating in victory at the Battle of Hastings. The tapestry famously depicts Harold being shot in the eye with an arrow, as he is said to have died — admittedly in what modern historians believe is likely a myth or artistic exaggeration.

This conquest was a crucial contributing moment in the establishment of what would become England and later the British Empire and the UK. It was the last of several successful foreign invasions of England in a millenium, and turned out to be the last one for a millenium.
The conquest also added the final core ingredient, French, to the linguistic melting pot that produced the modern English language.

The embroidered cloth, which has brief Latin titles captioning its 58 scenes, is widely accepted to have been made in England as a tribute to William after his victory. It was then transported to his family home in Normandy.

blocks.caption: England's last Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson saw off the Norse viking King Harald Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066, but riding south to deal with William the Conqueror soon after proved a battle too farImage: Pascal Deloche/Godong/picture alliance

articles.title: Iran says US strike killed four at wedding in 'war crime' as US denies targeting civilians
articles.summary: Iranian media reports two children were among those killed when shrapnel hit a home. Iran then launched missiles and drones at US targets in the Middle East.
articles.byline: Joe Coughlan, Claire Keenan, David Gritten

blocks.text: Watch: Iran and US exchange air strikes
ByJoe CoughlanClaire Keenan and David Gritten
Iran has accused the US of a war crime after officials said a missile strike killed four people including two children at a wedding celebration.

The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) said shrapnel from a missile hit a family wedding ceremony at a home in southern Iran, causing the deaths. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei called the incident a "war crime".
A US Central Command (Centcom) spokesperson said it "never targets civilians", adding that it was aware of the reports.
Iranian authorities said another 14 people were killed elsewhere. In response, Iran launched missiles and drones at US targets in Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Bahrain.
Most of the drones and missiles Iran launched at neighbouring countries were reportedly intercepted. Kuwait said a drone started a fire in a residential complex but caused no casualties.

Centcom said strikes on Iran followed "recent attempted attacks" by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against American forces and commercial shipping in the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway, through which around 20% of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.
The Iranian military's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters warned that operations against American forces in the region would continue until the US "regrets" its crimes.
Image source, Iranian Red Crescent Society
A picture distributed by the Iranian Red Crescent Society reportedly showing the remains of a building which was hosting the wedding ceremony
US President Donald Trump described Tuesday's strikes on Iran as "large and powerful".
Centcom said the targets included air defence sites, radar systems and maritime assets.
Iranian media reported explosions across the southern provinces of Hormozgan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Kerman and Khuzestan.
The IRCS said at least four people were killed and 67 others were injured when shrapnel from a missile hit a family wedding ceremony at a home in the coastal town of Kuhestak, in Sirik.
Citing the Hormozgan Governorate, Iranian media named the dead as Zarkhatoon Taheri, 50; Kolsum Mallahi Nazhdnia, 43; Mohammad Mallahi, 16; and Amirali Karimi, four.
Media outlets initially quoted the IRCS as saying that five people were killed.

"Unfortunately, this is a residential building. And unfortunately, this happened during my daughter's wedding ceremony," Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building, said in a video broadcast by state TV.
"It is a very saddening incident... Thank God the casualties were not higher."
Iran's parliamentary speaker and top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said it was another attack showing the US was "Satan".
Watch: What we know about reported strike on Iran wedding celebrations

BBC Verify confirmed that a video and two images taken on Tuesday near Kuhestak's coast showed the destruction of a telecommunications tower, and that other videos from Tuesday and Wednesday showed severely damaged houses about 130m (427ft) north of the tower.
BBC Persian Forensics, by examining published videos and CCTV footage, found the telecommunications tower was about 112m (367 ft) from the house where the wedding was being held.

A weapons expert also told BBC Verify that footage purportedly from the scene appeared to show remnants of an AGM-84 Standoff Land Attack Missile (SLAM_ER) - a type of cruise missile known to be used by the US.
Centcom spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins told the BBC it was aware of reports from Iranian state media of the attack in Sirik.
He added: "The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC."
Iranian state media reported that another seven people were killed in three separate US strikes around Ahvaz and Aqajari, in Khuzestan.

The IRGC meanwhile said that four members of its aerospace force, which oversees Iran's ballistic missiles, were killed by US attacks in Kermanshah, and that three members of the paramilitary Basij Resistance Force were killed on Lavan island, in the Gulf.

blocks.caption: Map of Strait of Hormuz

blocks.text: Early on Wednesday, the IRGC and the regular Iranian military announced that they had launched ballistic missiles and drones towards US bases in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates in retaliation for the US strikes.
They said the attacks caused casualties and damage at the US Marine barracks at Camp Titin on Jordan's Gulf of Aqaba coast.
Reuters news agency cited US officials as saying there were no casualties.
The Jordanian Armed Forces said they engaged 13 ballistic missiles, 10 of which were destroyed and three of which fell in remote, uninhabited areas.

The IRGC and the Iranian military also said that a maintenance centre, warehouses and equipment belonging to the US military were destroyed in Irbil, in Iraq's northern Kurdistan region, according to state media. Iraqi authorities did not comment on the attack, but local media reported that a US surveillance balloon was hit by drones.
In Kuwait, the fire service said its crews put out a fire at a residential complex that was struck by a drone and that no casualties were reported.
In a separate incident, the IRGC said two tankers caught fire after hitting mines while being guided through an "illegal route" in the Strait of Hormuz by the US military.
Saudi Arabia's national shipping company said two Filipino sailors were killed "in a security incident" involving its crude oil tanker SIDR as the vessel transited the waterway on Monday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vessels were visible across the Strait of Hormuz from Oman this week

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Vessels were visible across the Strait of Hormuz from Oman this week

After about a month-long pause, the US resumed attacks on Iran on Sunday, when it announced it had struck two rocket launchers to prevent them being used to lay naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at air bases in Jordan and a drone at the UAE.

The US and Israel launched a joint attack on Iran on 28 February, killing the country's supreme leader and other top officials at the start of a massive air campaign. Iran responded by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf with missiles and drones, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.

In June, the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) that called for an end to hostilities on all fronts and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. It also gave them two months to reach a final deal that covers Iran's nuclear programme, US sanctions and a permanent truce.
However, the MoU collapsed within weeks, leading to a resumption of hostilities.

Since then, both US and Iranian forces have fired on commercial shipping in the region, with Iran targeting vessels it says have sought to transit the Strait of Hormuz without its permission and the US enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Last week, the US had indicated that it was switching to economic sanctions on Iran, rather than military options, to try to win concessions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US economic measures.
Additional reporting by BBC Persian
Six months into the Iran war: What has Trump accomplished?

articles.title: Russia's hybrid attacks on Germany: When is it 'war'?
articles.summary: The German government is holding Russia responsible for an unsuccessful attack in Leipzig. Yet many feel that its response has been too mild.

image.caption: Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes like this one also take off from Leipzig, carrying military supplies for UkraineImage: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fortunately, nothing bad happened this time around. Had the attack succeeded, however, who knows what the consequences might have been: On the evening of August 4, a drone outfitted with explosives and a detonation device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes in the security area of Leipzig Airport. The airport serves as a hub for military aid to Ukraine.
The German government hesitated for a long time before publicly holding Russia responsible. But now the government has announced its findings.

On Tuesday, September 1, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that the methods used in the attempted attack were consistent with those seen in other Russian hybrid operations, citing the drone's construction, various components, explosives and detonation technology. He noted that the attack had been planned with a "high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort."

Back in late August, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said of the incident: "The federal government will make the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this." At the time, he did not mention Russia by name. And even now, Merz himself has not commented on the matter.

However, the price Russia will have to pay is relatively small. The Russian House cultural institute in Berlin is being shut down amid suspicions that it is serving as a cover for espionage. The Russian Consulate General in Bonn is also being closed. What's more, entry requirements for Russian citizens are set to be tightened, and Germany also plans to take tougher action against the Russian "shadow fleet." Exactly how and when remains unclear, however.
Mixed reactions to measures

For the environmentalist Green Party in the Bundestag, however, this does not go far enough. "The federal government's analysis came a bit late, and the steps it's taking aren't enough for me," said Sara Nanni, the Greens' security policy spokesperson, in an interview with DW. "I don't think anyone in Moscow is afraid or giving it a second thought right now." As an example, she said Germany should be taking tougher action against the Russian shadow fleet. This would be necessary to "stop the flow of money to the Russian war machine," she said.
Acts of sabotage linked to Russia surge in Europe

Roderich Kiesewetter, security expert with Chancellor Merz' center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is also dissatisfied. In the Handelsblatt newspaper, he called for the delivery of Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine — and for the activation of Article 4 of the NATO Treaty, which requires allies to engage into consultations in the event of an external threat. He urged the German government to abandon "the politically convenient path of appeasement."

However, wouldn't responding more assertively, as Kiesewetter demands, risk provoking a military confrontation with Russia, especially given that Russia flatly denies responsibility for the Leipzig incident? President Vladimir Putin called the German sanctions against his country a "serious mistake" and accused Germany of fabricating evidence. The Foreign Ministry in Moscow announced that it would take countermeasures.
Foreign Minister Wadephul sees Germany as a target

Once again, the question of whether Germany is already at war with Russia is being raised — and this time with even greater urgency. But the federal government has unequivocally denied it. "We are not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday, after he blamed Russia for the failed attack. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told German public broadcaster ARD that Germany is not at war but is a Russian "war target."

A year ago, in September 2025, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said — though without naming Russia: "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either." This came against the backdrop of increasing attacks on data networks, critical infrastructure and hybrid threats.

Security expert Sönke Marahrens from the University of Kiel offered a more nuanced answer: "No, Germany is not at war at the moment. We are facing hybrid activities by other countries, but we are not at war."

In Western countries, he noted, declarations of war are regulated by law. And in Germany, according to the constitution, the Bundestag must declare that the country is at war, and that applies only after a physical attack. "Nothing currently meets that definition," he said.
Ex-Lithuanian FM: 'We are on a trajectory of escalation'

However, Green Party lawmaker Sara Nanni fears that Russia will continue to escalate the situation. "We are not yet at war with Russia, but Russia appears to be preparing for a war not only against Ukraine but against all of Europe," she told DW, calling the incident in Leipzig an "attempted terrorist act."
Not at war with Russia

From a strictly legal standpoint, Germany is not at war with Russia. No declaration of war has been made, no recognized armed conflict exists, and no collective defense obligation has been invoked under Article 5. Furthermore, consultations among NATO members, which must take place before a collective defense obligation can be invoked, have not been scheduled under Article 4.

But things look different when it comes to hybrid warfare, which is not as precisely defined. Numerous security experts argue that Russia is already waging just such a hybrid war against Western nations. This refers to attacks on infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation and traditional espionage.

However, the line between hybrid war and an open act of war are blurry. Sönke Marahrens believes that Russia is using hybrid actions — such as the one in Leipzig — to advance its strategic interests in Germany, the second-most important supporter of Ukraine after the US. Had the attack at the airport been successful, it would have relieved pressure on the Russian front, Marahrens says. He went on to say that, "If Russia succeeds in convincing the German public not to support these political decisions (to support Ukraine), that would also directly reduce the pressure on the front lines."
The AfD factor and the Saxony-Anhalt election

The state elections coming up on Sunday in Saxony-Anhalt are one current example of Russian strategic interests. Many observers believe that this election is the most important in Germany in decades. The key question is whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which is classified as far-right by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution — will secure an absolute majority and, for the first time, govern a German state.

The AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine and would like to normalize relations with Russia. This resonates with many in eastern Germany, where the war in Ukraine is seen as none of Germany's business and where there is a feeling that too much money has already been sent to Ukraine.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?

This is why the federal government — composed of the conservate CDU/CSU bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — is being careful about stepping up its rhetoric, as doing so could potentially help the AfD secure an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt. On the other hand, it can hardly afford to place the blame for the events in Leipzig on Russia while also responding in only a relatively mild manner.
This dilemma may also be the reason why Chancellor Friedrich Merz has so far refrained from speaking out to blame Russia.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Austria women ice hockey team fight for future generations
articles.summary: Austria are getting ready for their first Women's Ice Hockey World Championship. But preparations have been overshadowed by a dispute about conditions, pay and getting men's cast off kit. A solution…

image.caption: Austria won an IIHF Division 1 tournament in China last year to qualify for this year's World Championship in DenmarkImage: Peng Zhigang/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: When the Austrian women's national ice hockey team took to the ice in the Women's European Cup of Nations in Slovakia last month, they did so without 11 of their top players.

Captain Anna Meixner and the rest of her team were frustrated that the Austrian Ice Hockey Association (ÖEHV) still hadn't responded to a list of grievances outlined in a letter to the organization last March. Meixner stresses that the players only went public with their complaints as something of a last resort.

Among the nine complaints on their list of demands were the standard of accommodation, having to change in unheated dressing rooms in the winter and not being paid per diems during training camps and international tournaments. They also said they had to make do with hand-me-down equipment from the men's team.
"We really tried to respect the federation (ÖEHV) and we really tried to solve it from within, without outside noise," Meixner told DW in a Zoom interview on Wednesday.
"So we had been fighting for four or five months without going out to the newspapers. But when we realized that nothing had changed, we had to take the next step."

"The final straw, if you want to call it that, was a camp last February. It was the no-heater-in-the-locker-room situation," said the 32-year-old forward, who, after two seasons in North America's PWHL (Professional Women's Hockey League) with the Ottawa Charge and Vancouver Goldeneyes, is returning to her previous team, Swedish outfit Brynas, for 2026-27.

"Here were people that had been sitting on a train for 14 hours, who didn't get food when they arrived. We had to go on the ice straight away. So, I think that was when it really became clear to us that enough is enough."
Fighting for future generations
Meixner also stressed that their aim was primarily to improve things for the women's national team in the longer term.

"We have this older generation right now and we're not going to play for the national team forever. We really felt it's time to give the next generation everything that we didn't have over the last 10 to 15 years. We brought it up with the team and everybody was on board right away."

To rachet up the pressure on the ÖEHV, the players also threatened to boycott the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship in Denmark in November – a significant moment, as this is the first time Austria have qualified for the top IIHF (International Ice Hockey Federation) tournament.

blocks.caption: Austrian captain Anna Meixner (94) played most of her two seasons in the PWHL for the Ottawa ChargeImage: Justin Tang/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Going to the newspapers," as Meixner put it, seems to have worked. In a press release following last month's tournament in Slovakia, in which Austria came second out of the four teams, the ÖEHV said it had taken the opportunity to hold "constructive conversations" with the players.
Now, Meixner appears cautiously optimistic.
Demands starting to be met

"We have gotten some answers from the federation and we are just in the process of going over everything. But now, we're happy about the direction things seem to be moving in," said Meixner, who added that the players and federation were finally speaking on an equal footing.

"It feels like they (the ÖEHV) actually want to change something. If it stays that way, I'm sure we can figure something out and make it work. Because obviously the last thing we want to do is to miss the World Championship."
Indeed, in a letter to the team sent on August 31, the ÖEHV responded to each of their nine demands outlining specific steps that had either already been implemented or were in the works.

These include a pledge to implement "clear regulations regarding per diems/remuneration and the timely payment of bonuses and travel expenses," to provide "adequate accommodation and reliable, needs-based catering" for training camps, "adequate cabin and gym facilities" as well as "sufficient time for travel and recovery."
Battling for 'bare minimums'
It also notes that it would seek a "teamwear solution" as part of a new contract with the association's equipment provider.
While this all seems promising, Meixner still finds it frustrating that in 2026, she and her teammates have had to battle so hard for what she termed "bare minimums."

At the same time though, she said that if the players and the ÖEHV do actually manage to put aside their dispute, it will be bigger than everything she has achieved on the ice – including winning the tournament in China last year that put Austria through to a first Women's Ice Hockey Championship.

"I'm unbelievably proud of us for staying hard at it for many months. There are so many girls from other nations reaching out saying, 'you know what? It's great that you're doing that and we should do the same," she said.
"We've heard the men's team stepping up, cheering for us. I think this is bigger than hockey. Hopefully this will be a big step for Austrian women's sports and Austrian women's in general."
Unless an unforeseen hitch arises over the next few weeks, Austria will open their first-ever World Championship campaign against Czechia in Esbjerg, Denmark on November 6.
Mathias Brück contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'Nothing but mud and silt' - the village swept away by deadly floods in Nepal
articles.summary: BBC South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri spoke to a local, who is still waiting for his his wife's body to be retrieved, as rescue efforts continue.
