articles.title: Watch: Moment Duane 'Keffe D' Davis is found guilty of Tupac Shakur's murder
articles.summary: The rapper's killing became one of popular culture's great mysteries, with countless theories but no arrests until 2023.

blocks.text: Duane "Keffe D" Davis, a 63-year-old former gang boss, has been found guilty of murdering rapper Tupac Shakur.

The famous rapper was shot multiple times on 7 September 1996 in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas and died several days later. Davis was unexpectedly charged with murder in 2023 and has been standing trial in Las Vegas.
Davis was charged with murder with a deadly weapon. He faces a potential sentence of life in prison without parole.

articles.title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
articles.summary:
• Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks

  • Airlink insist flyby conducted according to regulations

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets…

blocks.text: A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of around 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks.
The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

Flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41 to 46 feet (12 to 14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Airlink, a sponsor of the South African rugby union team, said that the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft travelling at around 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”

blocks.caption: The planes fly above the stadium before kick-off. Photograph: Gallo Images/Getty Images

blocks.text: South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over another stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But this weekend’s flyby was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.

blocks.caption: The second jet flies through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” said Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”
after newsletter promotion

Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said on Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.

“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.
Airlink said that the flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed that their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

articles.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
articles.summary:
Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination

A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the…

blocks.text: A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.
The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.
“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.
At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.

Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.
Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.

But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.

“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.
Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.
after newsletter promotion
Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.

“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

articles.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
articles.summary:
Pedro Sánchez says two countries are cooperating after mass incursion by 70,000 people into north African enclave

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has insisted there was no evidence…

blocks.text: Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has insisted there was no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions over immigration within the EU.
Although the overwhelming majority of the migrants crossed back into Morocco weeks ago, hundreds of people, including minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta, leading to tensions with residents.

Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure at Spain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities.
“There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday.

“Cooperation with Morocco is frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.”

The prime minister once again pointed the finger at “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco.

He also said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”.
Sánchez said that about 1,500 migrants remained in Ceuta, of whom 1,200 are minors, and there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave.

Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers.

Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.

articles.title: The most dramatic moments in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial, inside the court and out

image.caption: Lindsay Clancy listens to testimony from her former mother in law during her murder trial on Aug. 18, in Plymouth, Mass. (Jonathan Wiggs/Pool The Boston Globe/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children, infanticide and suicide.
On Wednesday, as jurors in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial started deliberating for a fifth day, a dramatic scene unfolded in another courtroom.

A 56-year-old woman was arraigned in Plymouth District Court on a charge of intimidation of a witness, jurors, or person in connection with Clancy's trial. Dawn Light is accused of filming jurors as they left the court a day earlier, not long after they'd told the judge they couldn't agree on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three children.
Light's attorney called it a "misunderstanding," and said she was trying to film Clancy.
Meanwhile, in the courtroom for Clancy's trial, Judge William Sullivan opened proceedings by giving a general admonishment about following his orders on how people should conduct themselves.

Yet, it was far from the first time the trial has been overshadowed by the frenzy surrounding it. Clancy's trial has gripped the public for the past five weeks, sparking debates about maternal mental health, launching online conspiracy theories and creating dramatic moments both inside the court and out as the livestreamed trial has generated intense interest.

Clancy, 36, is accused of killing her three children in 2023 while her then-husband was running an errand. Over the past five weeks, jurors at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., have heard that she strangled Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old Callan with exercise bands in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.

items: Deadlocked jury in case of U.S. mother who killed her kids ends 5th day of deliberations with no verdict

blocks.text: Clancy's defence doesn't dispute the killings. But they argue she isn't criminally responsible because she had bipolar disorder and was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and little-understood mental health condition that can affect a new mom's sense of reality.
Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder because she plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the killings.
Here are some of the dramatic moments that have unfolded since the trial started July 27.
'Crime junkie' arrested outside court
Let's start with the most recent: the woman accused of filming jurors.
In a statement to CBC News, Massachusetts State Police confirmed that Light was taken into police custody at approximately 3:40 p.m. ET outside the Plymouth District Courthouse.

items: Why Lindsay Clancy, on trial for the deaths of her 3 children, has so many supporters
How different would Lindsay Clancy's murder trial look if it happened in Canada?

blocks.text: A prosecutor said Light was parked in a restricted area behind the courthouse and is accused of filming jurors as they left court. Light told state police she was waiting to film Clancy and denied recording jurors, however, troopers found video of jurors in her phone's deleted-files folder, the prosecutor said.
In court, Light described herself as a "crime junkie" and Clancy supporter, according to the New Haven Register.
A not-guilty plea was entered on her behalf and she was released without having to post bail, but was ordered to stay away from the court, the jurors and any witnesses in the case.
Lawyer asks for mistrial
Another dramatic moment happened on Aug. 24, when a witness was reprimanded for bringing up Clancy's Catholic religion.
Dr. Kirk Heilbrun was recalling a conversation he'd had with Clancy in April.

"One of the things that she said when I asked about what happened, is that in the course of strangling each child, she said, 'Go to God, baby. Go to God,' " he said. "That was part of her expectation that she and the children would be together in heaven with God."

"She was raised as a Catholic. As I understand Catholic considerations, that's not necessarily what happens. But when I asked her about that, when I said, 'Isn't suicide a mortal sin?' " he said, before defence objected and the judge called the attorneys to the side.

Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, requested a mistrial, calling it "over the top." It also wasn't the first time the prosecution brought up the concept of "mortal sin," Reddington said, and suggested it was professional misconduct.

The judge denied the request, but later instructed the jury to disregard the reference to "the religion that the defendant was raised with," calling it "an absolutely inappropriate area of testimony."
Joe Tamburino, a legal analyst interviewed by CBS News, explained religion has no part in a trial and it was "completely wrong" for the witness to bring it up.
Reporter's credentials pulled for viral grin
Right around the time Sullivan denied the defence's request for a mistrial, CourtTV's livestream showed a moment in the media gallery that caught some observers off guard.

As the camera panned the room, a woman in a green dress appeared to smile at the camera, shrug and wink. The moment with the "green dress woman" quickly went viral, with people accusing her of being disrespectful in a triple-murder trial.

CBC News has viewed the footage. The woman was later identified as Brittany Romano, a freelance journalist meant to be covering the trial for Vanity Fair magazine. Romano has posted online that she was Clancy's childhood friend.
By the next day, the magazine had pulled Romano's credentials.
"We were interested in the prospect of a personal essay by Brittany Romano about her experience growing up with Lindsay Clancy," Vanity Fair said in a statement to the New York Post.

"Yesterday, after clear conflicts with our editorial standards and processes, we informed Romano that we were not moving forward with her essay and informed the court that she is no longer credentialed by Vanity Fair."

In a statement on Instagram on Aug. 25, Romano posted that "a smile is not a crime," adding that she smiles when she's anxious. She said she had received death threats and messages telling her to kill herself since her photo went viral.
How social media drives toxic obsession with the Lindsay Clancy case
TikTok witness not allowed to testify
Clancy has generated a lot of interest on TikTok.

One of the many people who posted about her in the leadup to the trial was Emily Thorndike, a former psychiatric hospital employee who worked at the same facility where Clancy was briefly committed before the killings, although she didn't work there when Clancy was there.

In a video she posted July 27, Thorndike, a social worker, said she "felt it important to address the lies and misinformation the prosecution is telling, particularly about McLean Hospital." In the 10-minute video, Thorndike claimed the level of care Clancy would have received was misrepresented by the prosecution.
The video has been viewed 6.2 million times as of Wednesday.

Reddington, Clancy's defence lawyer, tried to add Thorndike to the witness list. Thorndike appeared in a voir dire hearing with Sullivan, the judge, on Aug. 19. She spoke about staffing levels but also introduced herself in a way that some observers said undermined her credibility.
"I actually live in Brooklyn, New York, but I summer on Cape Cod. I'm spoiled like that," Thorndike said on the stand during the hearing, which was livestreamed by The Associated Press.
Sullivan ultimately ruled that her testimony was credible, but that she wouldn't be allowed to testify because, "mainly, this witness hadn't worked there for a year."
In a TikTok video that was later deleted, but has been viewed by other media outlets, Thorndike apologized for the comment, saying she "didn't get any prep" before going on the stand.
The prosecution's bows
In one of the more puzzling details of the trial, a lawyer for the prosecution has received attention for her hairstyles.
Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham has repeatedly worn bows in her hair — an unusual accessory in court.
While Buckingham has not publicly commented on her accessory, many commenters have suggested it's a tribute to Clancy's daughter, Cora.
During her opening statements, Buckingham noted that "Cora had just turned five. She was sweet, silly, smart. She loved sparkly dresses and wearing bows in her hair."
That day, Buckingham wore a black bow in her hair. She's worn them most days since.
Meanwhile, others have suggested the bows are an attempt to sway the jury.

It's a matter of contention online, where the bows have been called a cheap gimmick, cruel, taunting, "psychopathic," and "emotional abuse." Others on TikTok have called it "courtroom psychology," arguing that Buckingham is not seeking to torment Clancy, but to provide "jurors with a constant, silent reminder of Cora."
New Jersey defence attorney David Bruno told CourtTV he found the bows "improper" if they were indeed a tribute to Cora.
"That’s trying to inject her emotions or her belief into that case," he said.

On Wednesday, after a fifth day of deliberations, jurors once again told the judge they were still unable to reach a unanimous decision, and they were sent back to try again. The jury will return again Thursday morning.
If jurors ultimately can't agree on a verdict, the judge could declare a mistrial.

articles.title: Republicans back Trump in his trade war with Canada

image.caption: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, centre, arrives to meet with Speaker of the House Mike Johnson and Republican lawmakers at the U.S. Capitol in Washington on Wednesday. (J. Scott Applewhite/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Republican members of Congress are publicly backing U.S. President Donald Trump in his trade war with Canada and blaming Prime Minister Mark Carney's government for walking away from negotiations.
After meeting with U.S. trade rep on Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers defend president's tactics
Dozens of GOP House members gathered on Capitol Hill on Wednesday for a closed-door meeting with Trump's point man on tariffs, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

While some Republicans are quietly concerned that an escalation of costly tariffs could worsen their re-election prospects in the midterms in November, those who spoke with CBC News after meeting Greer generally expressed support for the president's trade strategy.
Trade war a campaign hurdle for some Republicans ahead of U.S. midterms
Texas Republican August Pfluger praised Trump for bringing manufacturing jobs back to the U.S. and pinned blame for the trade war on Ottawa.
"It's a war that is perpetuated by Canada," Pfluger told CBC News. "The Canadians need to get reasonable. They've taken advantage of the United States for a long time."

items: Carney says Trump and his cabinet should stop 'throwing shade' and get serious about a deal

blocks.text: Brian Mast, a five-term Congressman from Florida, also criticized Canada for the breakdown in trade talks.
"They were given the best possible deal, more generous than anybody else across the globe, and it's something that they turned their back on," Mast told CBC News.
When Greer emerged from the meeting, he did not respond to reporters' questions about the state of negotiations with Canada.
Trump criticizes Canada's banking policy
Meanwhile at the White House, Trump gave no sign of shifting his position that Canada has long taken advantage of the U.S. on trade.
Trump told reporters that one of his biggest grievances against Canada is the limits it puts on U.S. bank operations north of the border.

items: Donald Trump mistakes Bank of Canada for retail bank
Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost

blocks.text: "They basically don't allow banks of America to be in Canada, that's sort of emblematic of the way they treat us," Trump said in the Oval Office on Wednesday afternoon.
"Canada has all of its major banks here, and we're their biggest source of income, far bigger than they are in Canada," he said.
How Trump mastered the art of the distraction
On Capitol Hill, the sole Republican who raised concerns about the impact of the trade war on voters was Ralph Norman, who represents a South Carolina district.
"What I hear in South Carolina is affordability," said Norman. "It all goes into affordability, whether it's this [trade war with Canada], whether it's tariffs, whether it's housing, gas."
He says Greer expressed willingness to address how tariffs are affecting each state.
"The concerns, they were real," Norman said. "I think the White House will be listening."

items: Can the U.S.-Canada trade war change course if Democrats win the midterm elections?
Iran war hits 6-month milestone with Trump's attention largely elsewhere

blocks.text: Although polling suggests Trump's tariffs are deeply unpopular, other Congressional Republicans lined up to defend the president's trade war with Canada, in some cases repeating his arguments almost word-for-word.
Missouri Congressman Eric Burlison said it would not be a smart move for Canada to levy counter-tariffs on U.S. exports, as Carney has threatened to do next week.
"We're the economic powerhouse obviously compared to [Canada]," Burlison said. "I think Canada needs the United States more than we need them."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

articles.title: Pentagon makes testosterone screening mandatory for U.S. service members effective immediately

image.caption: The Pentagon released new guidance Wednesday for mandatory testosterone screening following a July directive from U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The ​U.S. Pentagon issued detailed guidance on Wednesday for a new, mandatory testosterone deficiency screening policy for active-duty and reserve service members age 30 and older, ‌a follow-up to a July announcement from U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
People aged 30 and up will be subjected to screening for hormone levels or disrupted menstrual cycles

The guidance, which is effective immediately, establishes standardized screening and treatment pathways for men and women that ​the Pentagon says are aimed at ​improving military readiness by identifying and managing hormonal and energy-availability issues.

Hegseth, who has promoted the use of ​testosterone, announced the mandate last month, raising questions ⁠among experts about whether ⁠there was a ‌scientific basis for such a policy. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration plans to hold a meeting of experts to discuss medical use of testosterone in ⁠mid-September.

items: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth unveils plan to test troops for low testosterone
Canada's top soldier expresses pride in 'who we are' after Hegseth targets cadets in post

blocks.text: According to the guidance, men age 30 and older will receive mandatory testosterone blood tests, while younger men will be tested ‌only on request or if clinicians identify warning signs.

For women, the guidance does not mandate routine testosterone blood tests, but it calls for screening for ​fatigue and disrupted menstrual cycles that can be associated with hormonal dysregulation and ⁠conditions called low-energy availability and relative energy deficiency in sport.
The ⁠document lays out guidelines for when it is appropriate to ⁠prescribe ⁠off-label testosterone in ​women, namely for postmenopausal women with unusually low sexual desire.

Doctors have ​raised concerns ⁠that broad testosterone testing could lead to unnecessary, or potentially harmful, treatment, saying there is little evidence that universal screening for low testosterone among military personnel would improve U.S. combat readiness.

articles.title: Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school

image.caption: Seasonal illnesses, and infections such as measles, could spread more this fall, as students 'who have been to all kinds of different places are now in close quarters again in classrooms,' McMaster University immunologist Matthew Miller told CBC News. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Health·New

With millions of Canadian kids heading back to school and temperatures set to drop, it’s time to brace for another fall of seasonal illnesses — and medical experts say staying healthy takes more than just a flu shot.
Families should consider 'suite of vaccines' to combat viral infections from flu to measles, experts say

The latest federal surveillance report, which tracks influenza, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), shows it’s likely the calm before the storm, with low and stable levels of all three respiratory threats that are set to come roaring back in the months ahead.

“As we transition to colder weather and we’re inside more, that’s when the bugs spread … and that’s when we see our emergency department visits start to go up, and then kids in the hospital more,” said Saskatoon-based pediatrician Dr. Ayisha Kurji, an assistant professor at the University of Saskatchewan.

McMaster University immunologist Matthew Miller says Canadians should already start assessing their options to get seasonal vaccines. For flu specifically, he noted that last year included a “really unusual severe early peak” in influenza circulation.
“We saw really high case counts in … early December, which is about a month in advance of when we normally see flu season peak,” Miller said.

“What that means is that it's really important to be immunized in a timely manner in the fall to ensure that our immune systems have time to respond to the vaccine and mount that protective immunity.”

items: Hospitalization rates for illnesses like COVID, flu have doubled since pre-pandemic, report finds

blocks.text: It typically takes around two to four weeks for the body to hit a peak immune response to the shot, he said.
And Miller stressed that a fall flu shot — which is recommended for all Canadians aged six months and up — is just one piece of the “suite of vaccines” families should consider.
Measles, for example, has continued circulating, and this fall may see further spread.

“Coming out of the summer months where families have often travelled ... puts everybody at increased risk when the school year starts again,” said Miller, “and all these young children, who have been to all kinds of different places, are now in close quarters again in classrooms.”
Mother urges parents to vaccinate kids after daughter’s measles death
Flu, COVID, RSV shots available for fall
Canada’s national vaccine advisory body recommends a COVID shot for higher-risk individuals, including older adults 65 and up and anyone who is pregnant or has underlying medical conditions.
“I still recommend the COVID vaccine because it’s still something that’s around, and still sends people into hospital,” said Kurji.
RSV vaccines are also available for older adults and pregnant individuals, to combat what Miller called an “extraordinarily dangerous virus to newborns.”

items: New data shows RSV shots prevent ‘most dangerous’ respiratory infection for newborns

blocks.text: Real-world research has shown these relatively new shots are making a huge difference in serious RSV-related illness, with one large study showing the vaccine given during pregnancy cut babies’ hospital risk by more than 80 per cent.
“It's really having a profound impact on reducing rates of infection and particularly severe infection in these age groups — older adults and, in particular, newborns,” Miller said.

Beyond seasonal vaccines, experts stress Canadians need to stay up to date on their routine shots as well, given the resurgence of a range of vaccine-preventable diseases like measles, which can lead to flu-like symptoms and a blotchy rash, or in more serious cases, pneumonia, brain swelling, or even death.

items: Alberta doctors urge province to offer free RSV shot to all newborns to cut health risks, hospital visits

blocks.text: “We have seen, since the pandemic, a decrease in uptake in the basic regular childhood vaccines,” said Dr. Joss Reimer, Canada’s chief public health officer.
“The recent spread of measles really shows us exactly what we need to be worried about,” she added.

“As soon as our numbers dip below a certain level, we do start to see these viruses come back and put children at risk, especially those kids who are either too young or, for some other health reason, can't get vaccinated.”
Group calls on B.C. government to adopt a universal infant RSV immunization program
Measles resurgence across Canada, U.S.

Just 85 per cent of two-year-olds in Canada were fully vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella by the end of 2025, federal data shows — a far cry from the 95 per cent medical experts say is needed population-wide to keep measles at bay.
The same data shows less than 80 per cent of children that age were fully vaccinated with the shot targeting diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough.
Middling vaccination rates in recent years have contributed to an explosion of measles, one of the world’s most contagious viruses, across North America.

items: No active measles cases in B.C., but health officials warn of new virus strain ahead of school year

blocks.text: The U.S. has seen 37 new outbreaks so far in 2026, involving thousands of cases, while Canada lost its official measles elimination status last November after racking up more than 5,000 infections since late 2024, and more than 1,000 new cases just this year.
B.C.'s provincial health officer Dr. Bonnie Henry recently said most of the 30 people hospitalized since the start of that province's outbreak last year have been unvaccinated children.
“It’s sad to me that’s that where we are,” Kurji said. “Measles is an illness that is highly preventable [through vaccines]… one dose is great, two doses is almost perfect.”

items: Surge in measles cases risks 'horrific' health consequences: immunologist

blocks.text: Most modern clinicians haven’t even witnessed a real measles infection in their lifetime, Kurji added, which means cases can be tougher to spot and precautions to prevent onward transmission may not be put in place fast enough.
